question.en: Given a search box's text, how would you find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters, and what are the time and space costs?
A reviewer sees the while loop nested inside the for loop and rejects the solution as O(n²). Are they right?

answer.en: No. The inner while only runs when the window must shrink, and left never moves backwards. Across the whole run each unit is inserted into the Set at most once and removed at most once, so the combined work of both loops is bounded by a constant per unit and the algorithm is O(n). The linear bound comes from the monotonic pointers, not from the shape of the loops.

question.en: The search box now receives emoji with modifiers, where one user-perceived character is several code points. Does Array.from(text) make the function count what users call a character?

answer.en: Not by itself. Array.from(text) iterates Unicode code points, which is already the safer choice over direct string indexing, which yields UTF-16 code units and splits surrogate pairs. But a grapheme cluster can span several code points (joined by zero-width joiners and modifiers), so one perceived character may occupy multiple positions in the window. Clarify with the interviewer which unit of uniqueness the product means (code units, code points, or grapheme clusters) and whether matching is case-sensitive before coding.

question.en: You receive duplicate records from paginated API responses. How would you deduplicate them while preserving first-seen order, and when would you choose Map over Set?
A teammate suggests replacing the whole function with [...new Set(records)]. Why does that silently fail for records merged from paginated responses?

answer.en: Because Set membership uses SameValueZero, and for objects that means identity: values are compared by reference, not by structure (MDN Set, https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Set). Each page is parsed separately, so the same record on two pages becomes two different object literals; neither equals the other, both are kept, and the spread returns the input with every duplicate intact. That is why the working version collects ids in a Set and filters by that explicit key.

question.en: Product changes the rule to last record wins, but each id must stay at the position where it was first seen. How does the approach change?

answer.en: Switch from a Set of ids to a Map<string, RecordItem> keyed by id. On each record, map.set(id, record) replaces the value of an existing key, and Map iteration follows the order in which each key was first inserted (MDN Map, https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Map), so [...map.values()] yields last-wins values in first-seen positions. State the conflict rule (first wins, last wins, or merge) before coding, because it changes the data structure, not just a line.

question.en: How would you traverse a nested menu DOM tree level by level to collect visible item labels, and why should a queue not use Array.shift() in a large traversal?
The indexed queue pushes every node and never removes anything; head just advances. A reviewer calls that a memory leak and proposes shift() to keep the array small. What is actually going on?

answer.en: It is not a leak; it is bounded scratch space. The array holds at most the visited nodes, O(v), and becomes garbage as soon as traversal finishes. The head index exists to avoid shift(), whose removal cost is linear in the remaining array; using it would make a large traversal pay quadratic queue costs. Trading transient O(v) scratch memory for quadratic time is a bad deal, and shift() does not even free the entries meaningfully, it reindexes the remainder.

question.en: The traversal matches selectors against node.children. What does it silently never see, and why does that matter for 'visible item labels'?

answer.en: children contains only element children, so text nodes are invisible to it, and it does not cross shadow-root boundaries, so shadow content is skipped. It also says nothing about layout visibility: an element can match [role=menuitem] while hidden by CSS or by an ancestor. The guidance is to define, before implementing, whether hidden subtrees, text nodes, shadow roots, and dynamically-added nodes are part of the traversal contract.

question.en: How would you memoize an expensive derived value used by a filterable list, and what correctness problems can a cache introduce?
Your memoize closes over a Map keyed by the argument. Callers keep the same array reference and mutate its contents between calls. What does the cache do, and why?

answer.en: It returns the stale cached result. The Map key is the argument's identity, and identity has not changed, so the lookup hits even though the data behind the reference is different. This is the documented failure mode of an identity-keyed cache: mutable inputs can change after caching. The fix is a contract, not a hack: prefer immutable inputs, or make the key an explicit version or token that represents every input affecting the result.

question.en: Product asks you to memoize the filtering so the first search feels instant too. What is wrong with the request, and what do you offer instead?

answer.en: Memoization only avoids repeating work for inputs it has already seen; it does not make the first computation cheaper, so a cold query is exactly as slow as before. It is also not a substitute for rendering only the rows that are needed: if the derived list still renders thousands of rows, caching the array saves computation but not rendering. Offer instead: measure before adding a cache, bound it when inputs like free-text queries are unbounded so stale keys cannot retain large results, and pair it with row-level rendering limits.

question.en: Implement a utility for a search input or scroll handler: when do you choose debounce versus throttle, and what production behaviors should the API specify?
Fast typists complain that debounced search feels laggy: results only appear after they stop typing. What knob is missing, and what must be specified before adding it?

answer.en: A plain trailing debounce has exactly one knob, the wait, so a long burst delays the first result until the burst ends. The missing pieces from the production contract are leading versus trailing behavior and a maximum wait: a leading edge fires early in the burst, and a maxWait bounds how long a continuous burst can postpone the trailing call. Decide and document which edges fire, keep argument and this forwarding, expose cancellation, and treat the actual numbers as a product decision rather than a universal constant.

question.en: You debounce a scroll handler that reads layout and writes styles. The call rate drops, but frames still jank. Why didn't the debounce help?

answer.en: Because rate limiting and frame alignment are different problems. Timer callbacks are ordinary tasks; a debounced callback runs whenever its timer fires, not synchronized with frames, so reads and writes can still interleave badly between frames. For visual scroll work the guidance is to keep the event handler light and batch the read/write work in requestAnimationFrame, so reads happen before writes inside a frame-aligned callback. Debounce may still be right for expensive non-visual work, but a timer alone does not guarantee frame-aligned rendering.

question.en: What should a deep-clone utility promise, and when is structuredClone() preferable to a JSON round trip?
structuredClone() throws DataCloneError on your state object. A teammate says: just fall back to JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(state)). What is wrong with that fallback?

answer.en: The throw is telling you the value graph leaves structured-cloneable data: functions, many DOM nodes, or instances with behavior are not cloneable by the platform algorithm. The JSON round trip does not clone those either; it is serialization, so it silently loses or transforms values instead of failing loudly: function-valued and undefined properties are omitted, Map and Set entries are dropped (they stringify to {}), Date objects come back as strings, and cycles throw their own TypeError (MDN JSON.stringify, https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/JSON/stringify). The fallback trades a loud, debuggable error for silent data corruption. The right move is to define the supported value graph and either scope the state to cloneable data or write a deliberately scoped clone.

question.en: Tests pass with a JSON round trip clone, but production state contains a Map and a self-reference. What exactly happens in each approach?

answer.en: structuredClone makes a deep copy that preserves the circular reference (the copy's self-pointer targets the copy, which is what the assertion copy.self === copy checks) and keeps the Map as a real Map. The JSON round trip cannot represent cycles, so it throws a TypeError, and it reduces the Map to an empty plain object, so the cloned state silently loses the filters. If the contract really is plain JSON only, serialization can be acceptable; the bug is applying it to state that is not plain JSON.

question.en: A route needs three independent API resources and may unmount before they finish. How would you run them, handle failure, and prevent obsolete results from updating the UI?
One of the three fetches rejects and Promise.all rejects immediately. Are the other two requests cancelled?

answer.en: No. Promise.all's rejection only abandons waiting for the remaining promises; the operations behind them keep running to completion, consuming bandwidth and resolving into nothing. Cancellation is a separate mechanism: pass one AbortSignal to every fetch and call abort() on route change or cleanup, and treat the resulting AbortError as expected rather than an error to surface. Concurrency (Promise.all), cancellation (AbortController), and failure handling are three different concerns.

question.en: You add an isMounted guard before every state update, so an unmounted component can never update. Is the stale-result problem solved?

answer.en: No, that only covers the unmount case. The classic race happens while the component is still mounted: the user moves from route A to route B (or types a new query), B's faster response renders, then A's slower response lands and overwrites it. The guard that fixes this is request identity: tag each load with a version, id, or the latest signal, and apply only results whose identity is still current. Lifecycle guards and identity guards solve different halves; AbortSignal-based cancellation reduces how often the race happens but does not replace the identity check.

question.en: Why can a promise callback run before a zero-delay timer, and how can excessive microtasks hurt a responsive interface?
A queueMicrotask callback schedules another microtask, which schedules another, forever. The page freezes. Why does such tiny work kill the UI?

answer.en: Because of the drain rule, not the size of each callback. After the current task finishes, the browser drains the entire microtask queue before returning to the event loop; if draining keeps enqueueing more microtasks, the drain never ends, so no timer, input event, or rendering opportunity is ever reached. Each individual callback can be trivial and the interface still starves. Keep microtasks short, yield between chunks of CPU work, and use task or frame-aligned scheduling for large or visual work.

question.en: A teammate wraps 'run after the screen updates' in setTimeout(..., 0), arguing the browser must have painted by then. Why is that wrong?

answer.en: Scheduling order and paint guarantees are different things. What the event loop promises is that microtasks scheduled during the current task run before the next task, so a promise callback can run before a zero-delay timer; it does not promise that a paint happened in between. A setTimeout callback can execute before the browser next renders, so 'timer means painted' is unfounded. For work that must be frame-aligned, use a frame-aligned scheduling strategy such as requestAnimationFrame rather than inferring paint state from timer order.

question.en: For a large document, how would you collect only text nodes under a content root while pruning subtrees marked as private, and what would you consider before choosing manual recursion?
A teammate simplifies your walker by returning FILTER_SKIP for [data-private] elements instead of FILTER_REJECT. Private text now leaks into the output. Why?

answer.en: For a TreeWalker, FILTER_REJECT on a node rejects the node and its entire subtree, while FILTER_SKIP skips only the node itself and still descends into its children. The original code relies on REJECT precisely so a private element's descendants are excluded; with SKIP, the walker does not report the private element but happily walks into it and accepts its text nodes. The distinction is real for TreeWalker; for NodeIterator the two constants are documented as equivalent and children are still visited (MDN, https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Document/createNodeIterator).

question.en: The requirement changes from subtrees marked data-private to anything the user cannot currently see. Does the TreeWalker still apply?

answer.en: Not as-is. TreeWalker filters see node type and attributes; they do not answer visual visibility. An element can be invisible via CSS (for example display: none on an ancestor), have zero size, or sit outside a clipped area, and the walker will still report its text. Visual visibility requires layout information, such as computed styles or intersection checks, which is a different mechanism with its own cost. Also re-clarify the other boundaries the contract must state: shadow roots, live mutations during traversal, and whitespace-only text nodes.

question.en: Design a utility that maps many browser tasks—such as image metadata reads or page prefetches—while never exceeding a caller-supplied concurrency limit. What guarantees should it provide?
Your mapWithLimit rejects on the first worker error. When item 7 fails, what happens to the tasks already in flight, and is that cancellation?

answer.en: Promise.all stops awaiting the other workers, but their tasks keep running: the operations behind them were already started and rejection does not reach them, so in-flight work is merely observed, not cancelled, and its results are never used. The design must state the failure contract explicitly: fail fast (reject and leave started tasks to finish unobserved), per-item outcomes (an allSettled-style report), or active cancellation by threading an AbortSignal into tasks and aborting on first failure. Fail fast and cancel the rest are different guarantees.

question.en: Why does the implementation spawn Math.min(limit, items.length) workers that pull indices, instead of simply starting all the tasks at once?

answer.en: Because starting all tasks at once is exactly Promise.all(items.map(task)), the unbounded pattern the utility exists to prevent: every fetch or metadata read would be in flight immediately, defeating the caller-supplied limit. The worker-pool shape is the guarantee: at most limit tasks are active at any moment, each worker pulls the next index when it settles, and results land at their original index so output order is preserved despite different completion order. The min() avoids spawning workers for an empty or short list. The limit protects browser and server resources; it does not by itself guarantee throughput or make individual tasks faster.
